headline: After a cold, dry Tuesday and Wednesday, a strong Thanksgiving storm brings 1–2 inches of rain, possibly damaging east winds gusting up to 60 mph in New York City and on Long Island (High Wind Watch 10 AM Thursday to 1 AM Friday), and widespread coastal flooding Thursday into Friday.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Tuesday is dry and much cooler as an unusually strong area of high pressure builds from the Great Lakes into New England, with highs struggling to reach 50 and mostly topping out in the upper 40s. Northwest winds gust about 17–29 mph in the city and along the coast from late morning into the afternoon, easing around 3–4 PM. Tuesday night is the coldest night of the season so far: mid to upper 20s inland, upper 20s to low 30s in most other places, and mid 30s in the New York City metro, which should stay just above freezing.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Wednesday is similarly cold and dry, with northeast winds and clouds increasing late in the day and at night ahead of a storm approaching from the south; Wednesday night is chilly but not as cold as Tuesday night. On Thanksgiving the storm tracks north from the Carolina coast, likely just inland somewhere between just west of I-95 and the Appalachians, and strong to damaging east winds are the main hazard, especially for New York City and Long Island, where gusts could reach 60 mph, most likely in the afternoon and early evening. A High Wind Watch covers New York City, Long Island, Hudson County and eastern Essex and Union counties in New Jersey from 10 AM Thursday to 1 AM Friday; confidence is not yet high enough to include Connecticut, interior northeast New Jersey and the Lower Hudson Valley, which may need wind advisories later. Rain spreads in from the south Thursday morning (afternoon if the storm is slower), turning steady and heavier in the afternoon and evening, with 1–2 inches expected and isolated totals up to 3 inches; the storm's fast movement should prevent significant flooding, though minor urban and poor-drainage flooding is possible, and rain tapers off late Thursday night into early Friday.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Winds ease considerably late Thursday night into early Friday as the storm moves north, then pick up again Friday from the west behind it, gusting 25–35 mph under mostly cloudy skies. Saturday stays breezy, with west gusts of about 23–35 mph and some low clouds possible. The discussion gives few details beyond Saturday.

coast: Coastal flooding is growing more likely with the full moon on the 24th and this week's King Tides; many spots need less than a foot of extra water to reach minor flood levels. Localized minor coastal flooding is possible with Wednesday morning's high tide, then widespread minor to moderate flooding is forecast from Thursday morning through Friday morning, with localized major flooding possible in the most vulnerable spots of the south shore back bays and western Great South Bay, and at a few New Jersey spots such as Kearny Point and the Hackensack River; how bad it gets depends on how fast and how far inland the storm tracks, which sets how long the east-northeast winds last. Beach flooding, erosion and overwash are all possible, though overwash looks isolated for now. On the water, a Small Craft Advisory on the ocean runs until 6 PM Tuesday with 5-foot seas and gusts near 29 mph (25 knots), followed by a lull into Wednesday before winds ramp up Wednesday night. A Storm Watch covers all coastal waters from Thursday morning through late Thursday night for gale- to possibly storm-force gusts, with gales possible again Friday and Friday night, especially on the ocean, and winds easing Saturday. Waves could peak at 15–20 feet on the ocean (occasionally 20–25 feet out east), 7–10 feet on Long Island Sound and about 10 feet on western Block Island Sound east of Orient Point, slowly subsiding but possibly still 5–8 feet on the ocean Saturday.
watch_for: Exact timing of Thursday's strongest winds and rain, and whether the High Wind Watch is upgraded or expanded inland to Connecticut, interior New Jersey and the Lower Hudson Valley.
Coastal flooding with the Thursday and Friday morning high tides, possibly locally major in the south shore back bays and parts of northeast New Jersey.
Minor urban and poor-drainage flooding with Thursday's 1–2 inches of rain.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in the cold, dry weather through Wednesday and in a strong Thanksgiving storm with wind, rain and coastal flooding, but less certain about the exact timing of the strongest winds and rain, how far inland damaging gusts reach, and how severe the coastal flooding gets.
